Credit Freeze Grips Pakistan’s Chemicals Industry as Firms Struggle with Liquidity Crunch

Pakistan’s chemicals industry is facing an acute credit freeze, with major firms reporting severe liquidity shortages as banks tighten lending standards in response to mounting sector-wide defaults. The crisis, which began unfolding in late May, has already led to production cutbacks, stalled investments, and the threat of widespread layoffs, according to industry representatives.

“Over the past three weeks, access to working capital has virtually dried up,” said Aamir Qureshi, president of the Pakistan Chemical Manufacturers Association. “Many of our members are unable to secure the short-term credit lines they rely on for raw material imports and day-to-day operations. Factories are running at less than half capacity.”

Multiple sources indicate that at least 18 mid-sized chemical producers have defaulted on existing loans since the start of June, triggering a broader loss of confidence among lenders. “Banks have become extremely risk-averse,” said Saima Raza, a Karachi-based credit analyst. “They are demanding higher collateral or simply refusing new credit requests from chemical firms, even those with previously strong records.”

The credit squeeze is being exacerbated by falling demand in both domestic and export markets, with buyers postponing orders amid economic uncertainty and currency volatility. Industry data shows that export volumes of key chemical products such as caustic soda and PVC have fallen by 27% year-on-year in May. Domestic sales are estimated to be down by at least 18% compared to last quarter.

“We are seeing a dangerous spiral,” warned Anwar Malik, CFO of National Petrochemicals Ltd. “Credit is tight, so companies are forced to scale back. That leads to job losses and further weakens demand, making it even harder to service debts.”

The Pakistan Chemical Workers Union reports that more than 4,000 workers have been furloughed in the last month, with many more facing reduced hours or unpaid leave. The union has called for urgent government intervention to stabilize the sector and prevent further job losses.

“Without immediate relief, we risk permanent closures and the destruction of a critical industry,” said Qureshi. Negotiations with government officials are ongoing, but as of Thursday no comprehensive support package has been announced. The situation remains highly volatile.
